content: Polymer fume fever, also referred to as fluoropolymer fever or colloquially as Teflon flu, is a condition caused by inhaling fumes released when polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) is heated to temperatures between 300°C and 450°C. PTFE is a synthetic polymer commonly known by trade names such as Teflon, Fluon, and Halon. When PTFE is heated beyond 450°C, the pyrolysis products differ, and inhalation of these products can result in acute lung injury. The symptoms of polymer fume fever are similar to those of influenza and include chills, headaches, fever, chest tightness, and a mild cough. Laboratory findings may reveal leukocytosis (an elevated white blood cell count), but chest X-rays are usually normal. The condition generally resolves within 48 hours, although this timeline has been questioned in some cases. It is important to note that the fumes released from PTFE at high temperatures are particularly toxic to certain bird species. Birds have a highly efficient respiratory system designed for rapid oxygen exchange, which makes them more susceptible to inhaled toxins that may not affect humans as severely.
